opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it surprised me a bit too when we started doing this work.

With supervised fine-tuning, the hard part is the data. To teach a model to use tools well, you need demonstrations: full trajectories where the model decides to call a tool, formats the call correctly, reads the result, maybe calls another tool, and eventually gets to the right answer. Collecting or synthesizing those traces at high quality is expensive. If your demonstrations have subtle mistakes or don't cover the situations the model will actually hit, the model faithfully learns those mistakes. You're also teaching it to imitate one particular path, when in reality there are often many valid ways to solve a task with tools.

With reinforcement learning, you mostly need two things: an environment where the model can actually call the tools, and a way to check whether the final outcome is correct. For a lot of agentic tasks, like answering a question from a database, fixing a failing test, or retrieving the right document, verifying the answer is much easier than writing out the ideal trajectory. So instead of carefully curating thousands of gold-standard traces, you write a reward function and let the model explore. It figures out on its own when to call a tool, how to recover when a call fails, and when to stop.

Another thing I like is that the model learns from its own distribution. In SFT you're pushing it toward someone else's behavior, which can be off-policy and a bit brittle. In RL, it's improving the behaviors it already tends to produce, so the learning feels more stable and generalizes better, especially for multi-turn interactions where small errors compound.

It's not free. You have to think about reward hacking, the infrastructure for rollouts can get complicated, and you usually need a reasonably capable base model so it gets some reward signal early on. But from a practical standpoint, building an environment and a verifier has been a lot less painful than building a big, clean demonstration dataset. That's why I've found RL the more natural fit for tool use.

r001.rationale: The response says SFT requires costly full trajectories with tool calls and results, but does not clearly say later calls depend on earlier tool results.

r002.rationale: It says RL needs an environment and a way to check the final outcome, letting the model explore without curating full demonstration trajectories.

r003.rationale: It says RL needs a reasonably capable base model to get an early reward signal, but does not attribute this to the model’s prior knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it comes down to data. With supervised fine-tuning, you need examples of the right behavior. If I want an agent to call a tool correctly, I need a dataset of trajectories where someone, or some model, did the right thing: picked the right tool, passed the right arguments, handled the result, maybe recovered from an error. And getting that data is really hard. Humans don't naturally produce agentic trajectories. You can't just scrape them off the internet the way you can scrape text. So you end up either paying people to painstakingly write out tool-call sequences, which is slow and expensive and they make mistakes, or you distill from a bigger model, in which case you're capped at whatever that bigger model does and you inherit all of its quirks.

With reinforcement learning, you flip the problem around. You don't need to know what the right trajectory looks like. You just need to be able to tell, at the end, whether the thing worked. And for a lot of tool-use tasks, that's actually pretty easy to check. Did the API call succeed? Did the test pass? Did the SQL query return the right rows? Did the final answer match? Writing a verifier is often way simpler than writing a demonstration. So you set up the environment, you let the model try things, and you reward it when it gets there. The model discovers its own way of using the tools, and sometimes it finds strategies you wouldn't have written down yourself.

There's a second piece, too, which is that RL is much more forgiving of the stuff you don't anticipate. In SFT, your data only covers the situations you thought to include. The moment the tool returns an error you didn't put in the dataset, the model's kind of off a cliff. In RL, the model hits that error during training, gets penalized if it flails, and learns to deal with it. It's learning from its own mistakes in its own distribution, rather than from a curated set of someone else's successes. That makes it a lot more robust when you actually deploy it.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. RL is finicky in its own ways: reward hacking, instability, you need good environments, and the engineering around rollouts is non-trivial. But that's engineering we can do. The data problem with SFT for agents is more fundamental. So in practice, what we see work is a small amount of SFT to get the format and the basic tool-calling behavior in place, and then RL does most of the real work of making the agent actually good at the task.

r001.rationale: It says SFT needs complete tool-use trajectories, including handling results and errors, but does not explain that later calls depend on earlier tool results.

r002.rationale: It describes trying tasks in an environment and rewarding verifiable success without demonstrations, but does not clearly state that training starts from prompts.

r003.rationale: It says the model discovers its own tool-use strategies, but does not attribute reasonable initial attempts to the model’s prior knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that with supervised fine-tuning, you have to show the model how to do the task. So you need demonstrations: here’s the tool you should call, here are the arguments, here’s what you should do with the result. And producing good demonstrations can be quite challenging, especially when there are multiple valid ways to solve a problem.

With reinforcement learning, you can often just check whether the task was completed successfully. You give the model access to the tools, let it try different approaches, and reward the outcome. You don’t have to prescribe the exact sequence of steps.

So you’re moving from having to generate a good solution to having to verify a solution. For tasks where verification is straightforward, that makes the setup much easier. Of course, the reward has to capture what you actually care about. But when you have that signal, the model can learn the tool-use strategy through trial and error.

r001.rationale: The response says producing demonstrations is challenging when there are multiple valid approaches, but does not explain that later tool calls depend on earlier tool results.

r002.rationale: It describes giving the model access to tools, rewarding whether the task succeeds, and learning without prescribing the exact sequence of steps.

r003.rationale: The response describes trial-and-error learning but does not attribute reasonable initial tool-use attempts to the models’ existing prior knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
For tool use, it’s often easier to tell whether the agent succeeded than to specify exactly what it should have done at every step. With supervised fine-tuning, you need demonstrations: in this situation, call this tool, use these arguments, and then take this next action. Creating those trajectories can be a lot of work, and there may be several valid ways to solve the task.

With reinforcement learning, if you have a reliable way to check the outcome, you can let the agent try different approaches and reward the ones that work. It can learn when to use a tool, how to interpret the result, and how to recover when something goes wrong. So the easier part is expressing the learning signal—you’re specifying what success looks like rather than writing out every step. That doesn’t mean the optimization itself is always easy.

r001.rationale: The response says SFT trajectories are laborious and allows for multiple valid approaches, but it does not explain that later tool calls depend on earlier tool results.

r002.rationale: It says RL can let the agent try approaches and reward successful outcomes when there is a reliable way to check the outcome, without requiring step-by-step demonstrations.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute reasonable initial tool-use attempts to the models’ existing prior knowledge.
